newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Outlook for Singapore home prices cloudy.
newsitem.headline: Outlook for Singapore home prices cloudy.

text.p: The outlook for the Singapore property market remains uncertain this year despite record bids submitted by developers at recent land sales, analysts said on Thursday.

Aggressive bidding by property tycoon Ng Teng Fong and Hong Kong's Li Ka-shing at the last two government land sales boosted sentiment, but the market remains weighed down by slow sales and looming expansion of supply, the analysts said.
"There are no signs of a pick-up. The current rate of sales is not significant enough to soak up supply which is coming on stream," said Lim Chung Chun, investment analyst with ING Baring Securities.
Lim said new supply of homes should total about 11,000 units this year and sales looked to be around 6,000 to 7,000 units, judging from the slower take-up rates of new homes in the last two quarters.
Despite the looming supply expansion and sluggish sales, interests controlled by Ng and Li tendered record prices at recent government auctions.

Through a private company, Japura Pte Ltd, Hong Kong billionaire Li submitted a bid of Singapore $682.8 million (US$484 million) or about S$457 per sq foot of building land for a residential site on the eastern part of the city-state at the start of the year.
His bid was at least 30 percent higher than the next highest bid and led many property analysts to question why he was so bullish on Singapore.
About a week later, local property tycoon Ng also made higher-than-expected bids for two residential sites. For both, Ng's bids were 18 percent higher than the next highest bids.
Some analysts said Ng's bid could have the effect of boosting confidence in the market as well as shoring up prices for some of his developments that were yet to be sold.
"Activity in the home market did pick up a bit after the news but it may not sustain," said the director of a real estate firm who declined to be identified.

"I am not sure about his (Ng's) reason for being so aggressive but it does not signal a turnaround in market conditions," said Liew Yin Sze, chief economist with J.M. Sassoon. He said general market sentiment was still soft judging from lower sales volume and slower housing loans growth.
ING Baring's Lim said private developers would also face stiff competition from the government's new upmarket public housing scheme, gaining in popularity among home buyers.

The government has said it will release land for up to 4,000 units of "executive" condominiums this year which come with facilities like swimming pools and tennis courts but are priced below private condominiums.
Analysts said that other than Ng's high bids, local developers remained cautious in their bidding.
Steven Choo, managing director with real estate consultants Jones Lang Wootton, said despite the current market lull, land sales would continue to attract foreign and local developers.
He said developers "could pick up a bargain" during this period. He noted residential land sales for 1996 were a record S$6.5 billion, with more than half from government land sales.
On the outlook for home prices this year, Choo said much would depend on Singapore's economic performance and when an expected recovery in the key electronics sector took place.
